title: Engineering in History
author: Richard Shelton Kirby; Sidney Withington; Arthur Burr Darling; Frederick Gridley Kilgour
note: Eligible sustained history and explanation of engineering, not specialist training. Use in a history course does not itself trigger H3. Broad cross-period account has no single central historical period, H13=0. Western scope is a limitation but not a single-nation history; T11=T12=0. No serious veto established. Mandatory Karpathy coverage; not promoted to the 200 merely because its small reader sample is positive. Original 1956 publication governs the age deduction, not the 1990 reprint.
notes: Established engineering history, but older scholarship and Western selection limit completeness and current historical confidence.
Relates infrastructure, power sources, materials, transport and industrial development.
Useful comparisons of changing constraints and engineering responses across technologies.
Explains components and their interaction in bridges, engines and other systems.

D=8/10, moderate confidence from contents, publisher description and detailed reader reports. Bridges, steam, canals and electricity add distinct knowledge; some chronological sections read as catalogues rather than connected explanations.
Historical mechanisms remain useful despite dated framing.
Directly covers engineering, infrastructure, energy and technological development.
Multi-author historical synthesis remains used in engineering history; authority is bounded by age and scope.
Logical chronological organization, with terminology and uneven transitions limiting accessibility.
Generally concrete technical description; older social assumptions need separation from engineering facts.

title: To Conquer the Air: The Wright Brothers and the Great Race for Flight
author: James Tobin
note: Eligible engineering biography and history. No serious veto established. American protagonists do not automatically trigger T11: the central technological race spans two continents and its principal influence is global aviation, so T11=0. Military and commercial applications are auxiliary to flight development, T12=0. Main narrative culminates in 1909; later biographical context does not reset H13. Mandatory Karpathy coverage; expert-praise selection is tracked separately.
notes: Archival biographical research and corroborating professional reviews support reliability; personal motives remain partly interpretive.
Connects aerodynamic experimentation, control, propulsion, institutional resources and commercialization.
Strong lessons in identifying the decisive problem, incremental testing and resource-constrained invention.
Explains the contrast between power-focused and control-focused approaches and the work needed after the first flight.

D=7.5/10, moderate confidence from Kirkus, Publishers Weekly and reader reports. Glider experiments, competing designs and commercialization add distinct cases. Family narrative and legal disputes can lower yield for readers focused on engineering.
Durable innovation history with little dependence on launch publicity.
Direct engineering and invention fit.
Historian and experienced biographer with substantial research; not an aeronautical engineering treatise.
Chronology and competing teams sustain a readable narrative.
Precise enough to preserve setbacks and uncertainty alongside dramatic episodes.

title: Life at the Speed of Light: From the Double Helix to the Dawn of Digital Life
author: J. Craig Venter
note: Eligible first-hand account of research and synthetic-genome engineering, not a technical curriculum or nutrition advice. The source reading report explicitly criticizes its teleportation analogy; a mention is not approval. No high-confidence veto established: documented experimental work is substantial, while future scenarios are speculative and acknowledged cellular-context limits constrain the DNA/software metaphor. Do not treat the book as proof that DNA alone is sufficient for life. T11=T12=0; biological engineering is central. Mandatory coverage, not selected for the praised 200 on the mixed reader evidence.
notes: First-hand experimental access is valuable; sweeping analogies and self-promotional framing lower evidential confidence outside the documented research.
Connects sequencing, synthesis, computation and laboratory organization, with thinner economic or institutional analysis.
Research bottlenecks and iterative troubleshooting offer reusable lessons.
Concrete engineering of genomes is explained; the pre-existing cellular machinery is essential and must not disappear from the model.

D=7/10, moderate confidence from contents, Karpathy's reading report and professional reviews. Reading, writing and transplanting genomes add distinct learning. Futuristic analogies and autobiographical emphasis can dilute the experimental account.
Experimental history lasts, while forecasts and contemporary frontier claims age quickly.
Strong fit for biological engineering, information processing and invention.
Leading participant with direct expertise, balanced against his personal stake in the narrative.
Research chronology is useful, but movement into speculative scenarios weakens the structure.
Software and teleportation metaphors can obscure necessary physical conditions.
